title: Display devices and the graphics pipeline
kicker: ENCT 201 · Computer Graphics and Visualization · Chapter 1
subtitle: How a description of a scene becomes a grid of coloured dots.

sections.title: Raster and random-scan displays
sections.body: A raster-scan display refreshes a grid of pixels row by row, 60+ times a second, from a frame buffer in memory; its memory need is resolution × bits per pixel. A random-scan (vector) display draws lines directly and only what is needed — sharp lines, poor fills. Flat panels (LCD, LED, OLED) are raster devices.

worked.why: A 1920 × 1080 display with 24 bits (3 bytes) per pixel.
At 60 Hz the buffer is read 60 times a second: bandwidth ≈ 373 MB/s.

choices.text: The colour of every pixel on the screen.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: The display hardware scans it continuously.

responses.title: It looks right at first.
responses.body: That is the display list of a random-scan device.

sections.title: The graphics pipeline
sections.body: Every renderer applies the same stages: a model (vertices and faces) is transformed into world space, then into the camera’s view, clipped against the view volume, projected to 2-D, mapped to the viewport, and finally rasterised — converted to pixels, where visibility and shading are resolved. OpenGL, DirectX, WebGL and game engines are implementations of it.

choices.text: At the end of the pipeline, turning projected primitives into pixels.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Earlier stages work on vertices, not pixels.

figures.caption: Figure 1.2.1 — the graphics pipeline
figures.note: Press Simulate: one triangle travels the whole pipeline.

sections.title: Graphics software and standards
sections.body: Low-level graphics APIs: OpenGL (and its web form WebGL), DirectX, Vulkan, Metal. PHIGS and GKS were early standards. On top sit engines and tools: Unity, Unreal, Blender and Maya for modelling and animation. Coordinates are usually Cartesian; graphics functions cover output primitives, attributes, transformations and input.

choices.text: A JavaScript API for GPU-accelerated 2-D/3-D graphics in the browser.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It is based on OpenGL ES.

sections.title: Applications
sections.body: Computer-aided design, medical imaging (CT/MRI volumes), scientific visualisation, games and film, user interfaces, simulation and training, virtual and augmented reality, and data visualisation. The same pipeline underlies all of them; what differs is the model and the speed requirement.

questions.prompt: At 60 frames per second each frame has about…

problems.prompt: Why must a game renderer finish a frame in under about 16 ms?
problems.answer: To keep 60 frames per second: 1 s / 60 ≈ 16.7 ms per frame for everything — transformation, clipping and shading of millions of triangles — which is why the work is done by parallel GPU hardware.

sections.title: 2-D and 3-D viewing pipelines
sections.body: In 2-D, a rectangular window in world coordinates selects what to show; the viewport is where it appears on screen; the window-to-viewport mapping scales and translates. In 3-D, a camera (position, direction, up) defines the view; a view volume (a box for parallel, a frustum for perspective) is clipped and projected onto a view plane.

worked.why: Window x from 0 to 100 mapped to a viewport x from 200 to 600. Where does x = 25 land?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It maps one rectangle onto another.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
• Frame buffer = width × height × bytes per pixel.
  • Pipeline: model → world → view → clip → project → viewport → raster.
